summary:
Bourgogne-Franche-Comté stands under the French national framework. Identity-document rules, anti-discrimination law, criminal law, marriage and legal gender recognition are set by national statute and apply uniformly to metropolitan and overseas regions, so the legal position of a trans visitor in this region is the same as elsewhere in France.

Detention carries the sharpest documented risk. France has no statutory rule governing where a trans prisoner is held: placement follows the gender inscribed on identity documents, and each facility improvises, using special units or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. A BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describes trans women incarcerated on that basis as falling into a legal grey area and being punished beyond their alleged crimes, with accounts of heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

The national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined around 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious violations of fundamental rights persisting across all places of detention: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and its recommendations now expressly extend to intersex and non-binary detainees.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was raised against the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, which argued that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at an airport, questioned in front of other travellers.

The Défenseur des droits has issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, and setting out official guidance for service providers. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination. National anti-discrimination statutes exist, but the country's own records show LGBT people remain targets of discrimination and violence, with reported incidents rising.

For partner recognition, the baseline is the marriage-equality law of 17 May 2013; France's first same-sex wedding was performed on 29 May 2013, days after the law took effect.

One restriction is documented within the region itself. The Côte-d'Or prefecture banned the Dijon Pride march from the city centre in June 2025. The march was not a first-time gathering: pride marches have been organised in the Burgundy cities of Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre since 2013, in a national pattern of marches spreading to provincial cities from 1994-1995 onward.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 legal gender-recognition reform changed French terminology and the framework for document amendment, but the CGLPL found no marked improvement in trans detainees' conditions between its 2010 and 2021 opinions, indicating that statutory reform did not by itself alter facility practice.

Formal anti-discrimination protection and lived outcomes diverge in official French sources: the national framework page records detailed statutory protections while stating that reported incidents of discrimination and violence against LGBT people are rising, and the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey puts identity-related discrimination reported by trans people in France at 64%.

The Dijon ban sits against national growth. Pride marches spread from the largest French cities to provincial centres from 1994-1995, and regional marches have run continuously in Bourgogne since 2013, so a city-centre prohibition in June 2025 represents a local restriction rather than a national pattern.

Isolation is documented across multiple jurisdictions in France, including the Tarbes facility holding Louna, which indicates that the placement problem is systemic rather than confined to any one establishment or region.
localsOnly:
French legal gender recognition is governed by national statute, as reformed in 2016, and applies identically to residents of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté; there is no separate regional procedure or additional regional requirement.

Residents and visitors held in places of deprivation of liberty can refer treatment complaints to the CGLPL, which has issued binding guidance to all places of detention following its opinion of 25 May 2021, and which accepts referrals from detained trans, intersex and non-binary people.

The Défenseur des droits issues framework decisions and guidance binding in effect on service providers across France, and receives the case files and association testimony on which its findings of persistent violations rest.

Regional Pride organising has a continuous local history: marches in Chalon-sur-Saône, Dijon and Auxerre have been held since 2013, so the June 2025 city-centre ban in Dijon restricted an established annual event.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in the inventory documents trans-specific placement decisions in prisons within Bourgogne-Franche-Comté itself; the detention evidence is national, and Louna's case concerns the Tarbes men's prison in Hautes-Pyrénées, cited here as evidence of the national pattern rather than of regional facilities.

The inventory does not state how the June 2025 Dijon Pride ban was resolved, whether it was challenged, or on what legal grounds the Côte-d'Or prefecture justified it; those points remain unverified here.

No source in the inventory addresses document-marker rules, entry screening at regional crossing points, or healthcare access for trans people within Bourgogne-Franche-Comté specifically. The border evidence is a single first-person account from 2017 concerning one airport and does not establish current enforcement practice.

Whether the Défenseur des droits framework decision cites case files from Bourgogne-Franche-Comté specifically is not established by the sources reviewed.
